evidence_set: REM sleep onset latency 18.0 min longer after alcohol than in the control condition (95% CI 8.8 to 27.1; prediction interval -18.8 to 54.8; k = 29, n = 212; p = 0.001); the delay grew with dose (meta-regression k = 28, n = 200, p = 0.024) and was not moderated by timing (p = 0.657).

Compared with the control condition, REM sleep was 11.3 min shorter after alcohol (95% CI -20.8 to -1.8; prediction interval -37.2 to 14.6; k = 13, n = 96; p = 0.026), more so with higher doses (k = 10, n = 64, p = 0.009); proportion of REM sleep 2.8% lower (-3.9 to -1.7; prediction interval -6.1 to 0.5; k = 32, n = 255; p < 0.001), not moderated by dose (p = 0.424) or timing (p = 0.664).

evidence_set: Total sleep time did not differ between alcohol and control (-10.1 min, 95% CI -24.6 to 4.4; prediction interval -71.5 to 51.3; k = 34, n = 284; p = 0.160), with no moderation by dose (p = 0.701) or timing (p = 0.488).

Neither wake after sleep onset (+4.0 min, 95% CI -2.3 to 10.3; prediction interval -12.4 to 20.3; k = 12, n = 166; p = 0.187) nor sleep efficiency (-0.7%, -1.8 to 0.3; prediction interval -4.5 to 3.0; k = 24, n = 203; p = 0.147) differed between alcohol and control, and neither was moderated by dose or timing.

Perceived time to fall asleep was significantly shorter after alcohol than control in three of five studies, with no significant difference in two; perceived sleep quality was significantly lower in two, higher in one and not significantly different in two.

82% of control-night latencies were already under 20 minutes, which may limit how much alcohol could shorten them; total sleep time was significantly reduced in five studies and increased in two, and many studies did not hold time in bed constant between conditions.

evidence_set: Limitations and future research, single paragraph running from p. 15; p. 16, left column, sentence beginning 'Finally'

Re-analysis restricted to the 176 of 307 walkers with a hangover: water drunk during the walk correlated with hangover severity before (r = 0.176, p = 0.019), during (r = 0.243, p < 0.001) and after (r = 0.229, p = 0.002), but not significantly with change in hangover severity (r = 0.103, p = 0.174; r = 0.017, p = 0.828; r = 0.066, p = 0.388).

Water drunk was not significantly correlated with thirst before, during or after the walk (r = -0.028, p = 0.714; r = -0.001, p = 0.993; r = 0.059, p = 0.435) or with changes in thirst (r = -0.023, 0.061 and 0.046).

After an evening of heavy drinking (amount on the study card), hangover severity was significantly higher than on an alcohol-free day at every hourly rating from 09:30 to 15:30, while thirst was significantly higher only at 09:30 and 10:30.

evidence_set: Compared with control, sleep onset latency 9.1 min longer (95% CI 3.8 to 14.4; k = 32, n = 280; p = 0.002); wake after sleep onset 11.8 min longer (2.5 to 21.0; k = 17, n = 148; p = 0.019); sleep efficiency 7.0% lower (4.0 to 10.0; k = 31, n = 274; p < 0.001); REM onset latency not significantly different (-1.5 min, -8.1 to 5.2; p = 0.581); none of these moderated by amount or timing.

Compared with control, light sleep (N1) increased by 6.1 min (95% CI 2.3 to 9.9) and 1.7% of sleep (0.2 to 3.1); deep sleep (N3 and N4) decreased by 11.4 min (k = 35, n = 127; p = 0.012) and 1.4% of sleep (p = 0.028); N2 and REM sleep did not change significantly.

Compared with control, perceived time to fall asleep was significantly longer with caffeine in 7 of 10 studies and perceived sleep quality significantly lower in 8 of 12, but none of 5 studies found a perceived increase in waking during the night.

evidence_set: Gastric fluid volume 19.2 (SD 14.6) ml with caffeine against 22.7 (SD 11.9) ml with placebo, and pH 2.12 (SD 1.63) against 1.91 (SD 1.24), both not significant.

Patients were randomized to caffeine tablets (amounts on the study card) or placebo tablets of identical appearance, both made by the pharmacy of the University of Basel, placed in blinded vials by an uninvolved anaesthetist and given by a ward nurse; no sequence-generation method or sample-size calculation is reported.

The authors suggest the tablets may reduce caffeine craving, improve compliance with fasting and reduce costs of postoperative morbidity; craving and costs were not measured, and no patient in either group took caffeine-containing drinks (plasma levels), so no gain in compliance could be shown.
